Long drought periods are typical, and the little rainfall that occurs is often in the form of short, violent storms or cloudbursts. The ground surface is generally baked hard, causing the rain to run off, or so porous that it fails to hold moisture. Flash floods are frequent. Precipitation is slightly greater and evaporation less in the Great Basin. Where rainfall is so light, dew formation assumes great significance. The yearly evaporation from a pan of water may be seven to thirty times the actual amount that falls on an area of similar size. The high evaporation rate correlates with low relative humidity which at noon may average less than 25-30 percent.
The mean annual temperature in the Great Basin is approximately 50°F, but it is over 68°F in parts of the desert scrub. Daily maximum summer temperature in the desert is 104°F or more. Differences between daily maximums and minimums are greater than in any other biome. Frosts are limited to mid-winter except in the sagebrush deserts of the Great Basin. The frost-free period averages more than 280 days. Frost and snow are common, however, in the Great Basin which, consequently, is sometimes called the cold desert in contrast to the hot desert adjacent to the south.
The Great Basin is not a single large unit. Rather it is broken up into a number of small ones separated by low mountain ranges running in a north-south direction and seldom exceeding heights of 6,000 feet. These ranges support pinon-juniper woodland. Water drains from the surrounding hills into these small basins from which there are usually no outlets. High rates of evaporation make the basin lakes very salty or may dry them up to produce alkaline flats.
